craft_claim: Major non-Anglophone traditions practise the reflective attitude in forms structurally unlike the English personal essay — Japanese zuihitsu and nikki (juxtaposed notings and diary) and Chinese rhapsodic self-reflection (Su Shi's Red Cliff) — establishing cross-cultural validity of the attitude without implying one universal form.

supporting_evidence.location: translation and scholarly apparatus, Columbia University Press 1967
supporting_evidence.note: The Pillow Book compiles first-person notings — lists, observations, and judgments of the elegant and the hateful — in an associational, evaluatively present voice; the edition documents the work as the founding Japanese instance of personal associative prose (zuihitsu).

supporting_evidence.location: ch. 14 (Shirane), 'The Pillow Book of Sei Shonagon'; ch. 15 (Arntzen), 'Heian literary diaries: from Tosa nikki to Sarashina nikki'
supporting_evidence.note: The Cambridge History treats the Pillow Book and the Heian nikki diary tradition as named, distinct canons of first-person writing (from Tosa nikki, c. 935, to Sarashina nikki), establishing a substantial non-Anglophone body of personal, reflective prose in Japanese literary history.

supporting_evidence.location: Whole composition: guest raises impermanence, host re-derives the vantage; 1082 Huangzhou exile
supporting_evidence.note: Su Shi's rhapsody turns a landscape visit inward through a dramatized question-and-answer — reflection as dialogue anchored in place rather than soliloquy — a Chinese instance of the reflective turn with different machinery from the essay.

supporting_evidence.location: Su Tung-p'o: Selections from a Sung Dynasty Poet, Columbia University Press 1965
supporting_evidence.note: Watson's scholarly translation collection provides the verified English-language anchor for Su Shi's prose-poem and its reflective-exile context.

counterevidence.note: Translation limit: Japanese parataxis and juxtaposition do not carry the analytic connectives (therefore / then I realized) that the English reflective voice relies on, and zuihitsu frequently notes without analyzing one experience inwardly — the mapping is analogue, not identity.

scope: Comparative support for cross-cultural validity of the attitude (inclusion criterion 5); feeds card section 8. Not a claim that any form is interchangeable with the Anglophone personal essay.
exceptions: Where a brief needs sustained Montaignean single-experience self-examination, zuihitsu is a cousin, not a template; Su Shi's resolution tips toward the philosophical neighbor.
